title: Broadway's Creative Teams
text:
A Broadway musical is made by a small team: composer, lyricist, book writer, choreographer, director and producer. Sociologists Brian Uzzi and Jarrett Spiro collected data on the creative teams behind hundreds of musicals that opened on Broadway between 1945 and 1989, and mapped who had worked with whom over the years.

The result was a network of artists connected by shared productions. Its shape changed from year to year. In some years, the industry was loosely connected, with teams made mostly of strangers. In others it was tightly knit, with the same people working together again and again and many connections between different clusters.

Uzzi and Spiro measured this closeness with a single number for each year and compared it to how well the shows did, both commercially and with critics. The relationship was an upside-down U. When the network was too loose, teams lacked the trust and shared know-how to work well. When it was too tight, teams recycled the same ideas and conventions. Shows did best in the middle range, when creative teams combined people who had worked together before with people from other circles who brought fresh material and approaches.
lesson: A team of old friends is comfortable but stale, and a team of strangers is fresh but clumsy. Mix trusted collaborators with a few newcomers.
source: Uzzi, B., and Spiro, J. (2005). Collaboration and creativity: The small world problem. American Journal of Sociology, 111(2), 447-504.
